messages.content: You are working in a lab and you have a sealed container with a gauge pressure of 2.5 atm. You are located at sea level where the atmospheric pressure is 1 atm. However, you need to transport the container to a high-altitude location where the atmospheric pressure is 0.85 atm. What will be the absolute pressure of the container at sea level and at the high-altitude location?

function.name: calc_absolute_pressure
function.description: Calculates the absolute pressure from gauge and atmospheric pressures. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

atm_pressure.description: The atmospheric pressure in atmospheres (atm). Default is 1 atm if not provided. This is a float type value.

gauge_pressure.description: The gauge pressure in atmospheres (atm). Must be provided. This is a float type value.

message.reasoning: We need to calculate absolute pressure at sea level: gauge + atm. At sea level atm=1 atm, gauge=2.5 atm => abs=3.5 atm. At high altitude atm=0.85 atm, gauge remains same? Gauge reading is relative to local atm. If gauge reads 2.5 atm at sea level, but gauge reading might change with altitude? Actually gauge pressure is difference between internal and external. If container sealed, internal pressure changes with external? If sealed container, internal pressure may remain constant? But gauge reading is relative to local atm. So gauge reading at high altitude would be internal minus local atm. If internal absolute remains same as at sea level? But sealed container might maintain internal absolute pressure? If container is sealed and rigid, internal absolute pressure stays same regardless of external? Actually if container is rigid, internal pressure remains constant. But gauge reading changes because atm changes. So gauge reading at high altitude would be internal absolute - local atm. If internal absolute remains 3.5 atm, then gauge at high altitude = 3.5 - 0.85 = 2.65 atm. But question asks absolute pressure at sea level and high altitude. So answer: 3.5 atm at sea level, 3.5 atm at high altitude if container sealed and rigid. But maybe they want absolute pressure at high altitude: gauge + atm = 2.5 + 0.85 = 3.35 atm. But gauge reading might change? They didn't specify gauge reading changes. They ask "What will be the absolute pressure of the container at sea level and at the high-altitude location?" So we compute absolute pressure using gauge + atm at each location. So at sea level: 2.5+1=3.5 atm. At high altitude: 2.5+0.85=3.35 atm. Use function.
